definition: A sum the parties agree in advance will be paid as compensation for a specified breach, set as a genuine pre-estimate of loss rather than a penalty.
origin: From Latin liquidare (to make clear, to settle an account), from liquidus (clear, fluid), paired with "damages," from Old French damage, from Latin damnum (loss, harm). English contract law used "liquidated" from the 17th century in its accounting sense of a sum made certain and fixed in advance, rather than left for a court to calculate.

definition: An equitable remedy compelling a party to carry out its exact obligations under a contract, ordered when monetary damages would be inadequate.
origin: From Latin specificus (of a particular kind), from species (kind, appearance) + facere (to make), combined with "performance," from Old French parfournir (to carry out fully), par- (thoroughly) + fournir (to furnish). English equity courts developed the phrase in the 18th century for ordering the exact, specific act promised, rather than merely awarding money.

definition: An agreement in which one party accepts a different performance than originally promised in full satisfaction of an existing obligation.
origin: From Old French acorder (to reconcile, agree), from Latin ad- (to) + cor (heart)—literally "to bring hearts together." English contract law paired it with "satisfaction" from the 16th century for an agreement to accept different performance in place of an original, disputed obligation.

definition: Evidence of prior or contemporaneous oral or written statements offered to add to, contradict, or explain the terms of a written contract, generally excluded once the writing is final.
origin: From Old French parole (word, speech), from Late Latin parabola (a comparison, a speech). Medieval English courts distinguished a sealed written deed from mere parol—spoken—promises, and the phrase survives in the modern rule limiting oral evidence against a final written contract.

definition: A promise by one party to answer for the debt, default, or obligation of another if that party fails to perform.
origin: A variant of warranty, altered under the influence of French garantir and Spanish garantía, all tracing to the same Germanic root warjan (to defend, protect) that gives English "ward." Merchants and lawyers used the "g" spelling from the 17th century for a promise to answer for another party's debt if they failed to pay.

origin: From Old French assigner (to allot, appoint), from Latin assignare, ad- (to) + signare (to mark out, seal). Property law adopted the term in the 14th century for formally "marking out" and transferring a right or interest to someone else.

definition: The automatic discharge of a contract when an unforeseen event, through no fault of either party, makes performance impossible or radically different from what was agreed.
origin: From Latin frustratio (a deception, a disappointment), from frustrari (to deceive, frustrate), from frustra (in vain). English contract law adopted the everyday sense of thwarted effort in the early 20th century, most notably after a 1903 English case about a cancelled coronation procession, for a doctrine discharging contracts made impossible by unforeseen events.

definition: The direct legal relationship between the parties to a contract that generally allows only those parties to sue or be sued on it.
origin: From Old French privete (privacy, a private matter), from Latin privatus (private, restricted to an individual). English contract law adopted the term by the 16th century for the private, direct bond linking only the actual parties to an agreement, excluding outsiders from suing on it.
